sm: The Williamson County Education Committee meeting was called to order at four thirty with a hard stop at five thirty. The minutes were approved by voice vote. Interim Superintendent Dr. Webb then reported on the five-year capital plan, which goes to the school board and the commission each year. She said the middle school on Split Log was originally set at forty-five and a half million dollars from education impact fee funds. About fifteen million will be drawn in the first year, with the rest left to earn interest and drawn only as needed. That fund takes in roughly nineteen to twenty million a year, and the pace will follow growth in the area. She then introduced the question of when to move Fairview Elementary, built in 1962, forward in the plan, with the school board vote pushed to December seventh.

Dr. Webb said more than twenty developments have been pulled in Fairview, anticipating over three thousand new homes. Enrollment is not yet pressing, though. Fairview Elementary is at sixty-one percent capacity with four hundred four students, and Westwood Elementary is at seventy-two percent with about five hundred fifty. She said a possible essential housing project for county employees on the adjacent land could bring cost savings. Merging the two schools would exceed the board's limit of nine hundred forty students for an elementary school. She listed the upgrades made to Fairview, including sewer line lining, a new lift station, a new roof, new rooftop air conditioning in 2025, and a 1.8 million dollar renovation in 2017. Commissioners voiced support for a replacement, and Dr. Webb said the building is in good working order and instruction has not been affected.

Dr. Webb explained that impact fees cannot be used yet because the district would need to show its elementary schools are at or near capacity, in the high nineties or more. The district has ten point eight million dollars in federal tax credit money in its account for capital projects, and expects about five million more next year. A commissioner asked why the project is becoming a priority at fifty-five to sixty percent capacity. Dr. Webb said it is the building's age and community interest, and she noted the district has held land for years before building, as with a past middle school site. Members explained that the recent plumbing backups were caused by things flushed down toilets and not by poor repair work. Dr. Webb said that the district will recommend uses for any vacated space within six months. The chair then invited school board members to share their views.

Board members spoke about their tour of Fairview the previous Friday. Several said the school was clean, bright and well kept, and comparable to other elementary schools in the district. One member said that, with impact fees unavailable and a significant budget gap ahead, the district should not pursue it now. Tonya Hibma said she does not want to put a wish in the five-year plan and asked what budget the commission could offer, adding that growth could justify it later. Tracy Anderson noted that developers have paid impact fees countywide since 2017. She said the last elementary school cost about thirty-five million dollars, while this one is projected at fifty-five million. Without impact fees the county would have to issue a bond. She also asked whether the planned county employee housing could offset costs if timed with the school.

Discussion continued on the employee housing project, expected to have about two hundred fifty units, likely with many elementary-age children. A third party would build it at no expense to the county under a fifty-five year lease, after which the county would own the buildings. Timing from start to finish was estimated at twenty-four to thirty-six months, and any savings from building the school at the same time would have to be negotiated. Ms. Anderson said aligning the two could be a win-win, possibly using the ten million dollars in tax credit funds to reduce a bond. One commissioner, an army engineer, said the school is safe and well kept, and preferred to pay as you go. The chair thanked the board members and said the commission and school board are partners working together.

The chair closed the discussion and moved on to resolutions. The first amended the 2026-2027 capital fund budget by ten million eight hundred sixty-four thousand dollars for an energy investment tax credit from geothermal systems at Page High, Amanda North Elementary and Errington Elementary. It passed unanimously. The second was an inter-category adjustment of about twelve thousand dollars for approved raises of two, four and five percent, and it also passed unanimously. Three resolutions followed appropriating money from fund balance to the county self-insurance fund for unanticipated medical costs of school employees, at one thousand dollars per full-time equivalent: one for the general fund, one of one hundred fifty-six thousand dollars for the cafeteria fund, and one of sixty-three thousand dollars for extended school year. All three passed unanimously. The fund balance is just below three percent, and one commissioner said the cost was foreseeable. The meeting then adjourned.
